items.title: In un video il lutto di una megattera che veglia il suo cucciolo
items.summary: Il raro avvistamento documentato al largo della costa australiana
items.content: Anche le megattere vivono il lutto : lo dimostrano le immagini di una femmina ripresa in Australia mentre veglia il suo piccolo nato morto . Il raro avvistamento al largo della Gold Coast meridionale è stato documentato in un video dai ricercatori della Griffith University e della Sea World Foundation, che pubblicano il loro studio sulla rivista Discover Animals. Secondo quanto afferma Olaf Meynecke, del programma di ricerca su balene e clima della Griffith University, i comportamenti di attenzione post-mortem nei cetacei erano stati finora documentati prevalentemente tra i cetacei muniti di denti e i delfinidi (noti come odontoceti), ma erano rimasti in gran parte assenti dalla letteratura scientifica riguardante i misticeti (balene con i fanoni) come le megattere. "A differenza dei casi segnalati tra gli odontoceti, in cui le madri sono state viste sollevare i piccoli morti verso la superficie, questa megattera ha mostrato comportamenti e attenzioni prolungati verso il piccolo deceduto stando sotto il pelo dell'acqua ", spiega l'esperto. " È rimasta vicino al piccolo , mantenendo il contatto visivo e posizionandosi accanto a lui per diverse ore e forse anche per giorni. Questi comportamenti osservati sono coerenti con azioni di cura e accudimento , nonché con risposte di attenzione post-mortem documentate in mammiferi dalla struttura sociale complessa, e indicano un forte attaccamento materno innato verso il piccolo". "Questo caso di studio - aggiunge Meynecke - evidenzia la necessità di una documentazione sistematica e continua dei rari eventi di mortalità neonatale, al fine di comprendere meglio il significato cognitivo, emotivo ed evolutivo dei comportamenti post-mortem nelle grandi balene".

items.title: È il giorno della sentenza di primo grado sull’omicidio di Giulio Regeni
items.summary: La pronuncerà la Corte d'Assise di Roma, a più di dieci anni da quando il ricercatore italiano fu sequestrato, torturato e ucciso in Egitto
items.content:
Lunedì mattina, al tribunale di Roma di piazzale Clodio, è iniziata l’udienza in cui la Corte d’Assise pronuncerà la sentenza di primo grado nel processo sul sequestro e sull’omicidio di Giulio Regeni, il ricercatore italiano torturato e ucciso in Egitto nel 2016. Paola Deffendi e Claudio Regeni, i genitori di Giulio, sono entrati alle 9:15 in aula, accompagnati dall’avvocata Alessandra Ballerini. Appena dopo l’inizio dell’udienza, intorno alle 10:15, i giudici l’hanno rinviata alle 18 e sono andati in camera di consiglio per decidere.

Fuori dal tribunale Ballerini ha ringraziato i giornalisti e il “popolo giallo”, i sostenitori e le sostenitrici della campagna “Verità e giustizia per Giulio Regeni”, e ha detto che «siamo qui oggi nonostante questo faticosissimo percorso a ostacoli, in salita. In pochi avrebbero scommesso che saremmo arrivati a un processo e poi a una sentenza. Tutto quello che il regime poteva mettere in campo per impedire questo processo lo ha fatto. Però questa famiglia è forte e resistente. I Regeni hanno combattuto per noi e se oggi i nostri diritti valgono un po’ di più è merito loro».

Da sinistra: Gianni Cuperlo, Claudio Regeni, Alessandra Ballerini, Paola Deffendi, Irene Regeni e, parzialmente coperta, Elly Schlein, con lo striscione davanti al tribunale, Roma, 28 settembre 2026 (ANSA/RICCARDO ANTIMIANI)

Prima dell’udienza si è presentata anche la segretaria del Partito Democratico, Elly Schlein, che segue il processo Regeni da tempo. Nell’aula gremita c’erano anche il deputato del PD Gianni Cuperlo e l’europarlamentare del PD Annalisa Corrado. Le prime file erano occupate da persone che indossavano magliette e spille gialle.

La sentenza arriverà dopo dieci anni e mezzo di depistaggi, tensioni diplomatiche, intoppi processuali e una mobilitazione civile con pochi eguali in Italia.

Gli imputati sono quattro agenti dei servizi di sicurezza interni egiziani e, come è avvenuto per tutto il processo, nemmeno oggi si sono presentati in aula. Sono formalmente irreperibili perché l’Egitto si è sempre rifiutato di fornire all’Italia i loro indirizzi a cui recapitare gli atti processuali. Il processo era iniziato a ottobre del 2021 ed era poi stato sospeso: si è infine potuto svolgere nel 2024, grazie a un’ importante sentenza della Corte costituzionale dell’anno prima.

Paola Deffendi e Claudio Regeni, i genitori di Giulio Regeni, arrivano nell’aula Occorsio accompagnati dall’avvocata Alessandra Ballerini. Dentro all’aula ci sono varie persone che indossano spille e braccialetti gialli con la scritta “Verità e giustizia per Giulio Regeni”, che salutano subito la famiglia Regeni. Roma, 28 settembre (Laura Fasani/Il Post)

Il generale Tariq Sabir, i colonnelli Athar Kamel Mohamed Ibrahim e Uhsam Helmi, e il generale Magdi Ibrahim Abdelal Sharif sono accusati di sequestro di persona pluriaggravato. Sharif deve rispondere anche di lesioni personali aggravate e di omicidio aggravato, in concorso con altre persone mai identificate. Per lui la procura di Roma ha chiesto la condanna all’ergastolo, per gli altri tre 17 anni e sei mesi di carcere.

Il governo italiano si è anche costituito parte civile al processo e l’avvocatura di Stato ha chiesto agli imputati un risarcimento di due milioni di euro, perché con il sequestro e l’uccisione di Giulio Regeni è stato leso anche il diritto dello Stato di proteggere i propri cittadini anche all’estero. Se dunque la Corte d’Assise dovesse condannare gli imputati anche solo per un capo d’imputazione, potrebbe essere chiamato a rispondere dei danni anche l’Egitto, dal momento che gli imputati sono funzionari pubblici.

In caso di condanna definitiva, inoltre, l’Italia dovrebbe chiedere all’Egitto di eseguirla: è assai improbabile che succeda, ma la richiesta stessa avrebbe inevitabili conseguenze diplomatiche.

Giulio Regeni era nato il 15 gennaio 1988 a Fiumicello Villa Vicentina, un piccolo comune in provincia di Udine, in Friuli Venezia Giulia, a pochi chilometri dal confine con la Slovenia. Dal 2014 era un dottorando dell’università di Cambridge, in Inghilterra, ed era arrivato per la prima volta in Egitto nel settembre del 2015 per una ricerca sui sindacati indipendenti dei venditori ambulanti.

Scomparve la sera del 25 gennaio 2016. Le indagini ricostruirono che il cellulare di Regeni si agganciò alla cella della fermata metropolitana Dokki, la più vicina a casa sua, vicina a piazza Tahrir, la principale del Cairo. Doveva incontrare quella sera Gennaro Gervasio, un professore diventato suo amico. Gervasio provò a chiamarlo più volte, senza successo. Fu lui ad avvertire le autorità italiane, che per alcuni giorni chiesero alla famiglia di Regeni di mantenere la riservatezza sulla scomparsa di Giulio.

Regeni fu trovato morto il 3 febbraio lungo la strada che dal Cairo porta ad Alessandria, sul cavalcavia Hazem Hassan. Era nudo dalla vita in giù e reso irriconoscibile dalle torture. Aveva le costole rotte, fratture ovunque, denti rotti, bruciature di sigaretta qua e là sul corpo, lesioni alla testa, al volto, alle gambe e sulle piante dei piedi. L’autopsia stabilì poi che le lesioni erano state provocate in momenti diversi, con bastoni, coltelli e mazze, e che Regeni era morto per la frattura di una vertebra cervicale. Fu quindi torturato per giorni e poi ucciso.

Persone che indossano spille e braccialetti gialli in sostegno a Giulio Regeni salutano Paola Deffendi e Claudio Regeni (Laura Fasani/il Post)

Sua madre, Paola Deffendi, raccontando di quando vide il corpo per la prima volta, disse che «era Giulio, ma non era Giulio», da quanto era stato sfigurato. Anche l’ex ambasciatore italiano in Egitto Maurizio Massari, che riuscì a vedere Regeni in obitorio al Cairo, disse che non aveva mai visto niente di simile.

Le autorità egiziane cercarono di far passare l’uccisione di Regeni prima come un incidente stradale, poi come un omicidio avvenuto nel corso di una relazione omosessuale, poi come un regolamento di conti tra trafficanti di droga. I tentativi di depistaggio furono molti, tanto che durante la requisitoria del 23 giugno scorso il procuratore aggiunto Sergio Colaiocco ha detto che «questo è stato un processo contro la menzogna e le ricostruzioni artificiose».

Una delle più clamorose risale a marzo del 2016, quando l’Egitto annunciò di aver risolto il caso e che i colpevoli erano quattro membri di una banda criminale: erano stati tutti uccisi in uno scontro a fuoco con la polizia, dunque nessuno poteva dare la sua versione. In casa di uno dei componenti del presunto gruppo criminale furono trovati i documenti di Regeni: solo in seguito fu appurato che erano stati posizionati lì da qualcun altro.

Secondo quanto ricostruito dalla procura di Roma fu invece un leader del sindacato dei venditori ambulanti, Mohammed Abdallah, a denunciare le attività di Regeni ai servizi segreti interni egiziani. Fu sempre Abdallah a filmare i suoi incontri con Regeni per conto dei servizi all’inizio del 2016. Quei filmati furono poi acquisiti dagli investigatori italiani e rivelarono i contatti di Abdallah con i servizi, fornendo una prova importantissima al processo. Si possono vedere anche nel documentario Giulio Regeni – Tutto il male del mondo , distribuito nei cinema italiani lo scorso febbraio e disponibile online su Sky e NOW.

Per via delle sue ricerche Regeni aveva molti contatti con i sindacati egiziani e con attivisti antigovernativi: è possibile che i servizi egiziani si fossero convinti, a torto, che Regeni fosse una spia, o che la sua attività di ricerca con i sindacati potesse essere in qualche modo pericolosa e destabilizzante per il regime.

Gli investigatori italiani riuscirono a risalire ai componenti dei servizi anche grazie ai testimoni reperiti da Ballerini. Questi testimoni permisero di ricostruire che Regeni dopo il sequestro era stato portato a Lazoughly, un edificio del ministero dell’Interno al Cairo dove i detenuti venivano torturati.

I vari tentativi di depistaggio indussero a un certo punto il governo italiano a richiamare in Italia l’ambasciatore Massari. Nell’agosto del 2017, dopo circa un anno di assenza e in seguito a una maggiore collaborazione da parte della procura di Giza, il governo Gentiloni nominò però un nuovo ambasciatore in Egitto, Giampaolo Cantini. Nel tempo l’Italia e l’Egitto hanno ripreso i rapporti. A inizio settembre il ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani ha incontrato il suo omologo egiziano, Badr Abdelatty, per firmare due accordi di cooperazione: su X Tajani ha scritto che «Italia ed Egitto hanno rapporti politici solidi. Vogliamo trasformarli sempre più in crescita e investimenti per i nostri cittadini».

items.title: Bill Gates: 'Gli Usa prendano la guida sulla regolamentazione dell'IA'
items.summary: 'L'autoregolamentazione non basta. Necessario che Washington approvi una legge'
items.content:
Il cofondatore di Microsoft e miliardario filantropo Bill Gates ha esortato gli Stati Uniti ad assumere un ruolo guida nella regolamentazione della crescita dell'IA, avvertendo però che raggiungere un accordo internazionale su un quadro normativo globale potrebbe rivelarsi "più difficile" rispetto ai negoziati dell'era della Guerra Fredda per la limitazione delle armi nucleari. Parlando a 'Meet the Press' di Nbc, Gates ha detto che "nessuno pensa che l'autoregolamentazione basti. Quindi è necessario che a Washington venga approvata una legge".

"L'IA è certamente abbastanza potente da innescare eventi che causano un miliardo di morti, no? Quindi, anche se è piuttosto difficile raggiungere una certezza assoluta, non c'è mai stata un'arma potente quanto la combinazione di individui malintenzionati che usano i più recenti strumenti di IA", ha detto Gates, in una valutazione fatta durante l'intervista anticipata da Nbc nei giorni scorsi. Gates ha criticato l'approccio dell'amministrazione Trump, che considera l'IA esclusivamente nell'ottica di competizione globale con la Cina, trascurandone i rischi esistenziali per la sicurezza. All'inizio del mese, Donald Trump ha respinto le richieste affinché il governo federale imponesse dei vincoli alle aziende che sviluppano modelli di IA, affermando in un post su Truth Social: "CHI VINCE NELL'IA, VINCE! Siamo in vantaggio sulla Cina e su tutti gli altri, e continueremo a esserlo". "Ciò che ha detto è legittimo, ma credo che, dopo aver ascoltato me e altre persone, e aver capito che questo non ci svantaggia in quella che lui percepisce come una competizione tra nazioni, si arriverà a un consenso", ha affermato. In seguito, Gates ha citato altri casi in cui gli Stati Uniti hanno guidato il mondo nella definizione di accordi di ampia portata a tutela dell'umanità. "Dalla Seconda guerra mondiale a oggi, gli Stati Uniti possono andare molto fieri di come hanno affrontato le sfide globali: lo abbiamo fatto in modo costruttivo, coinvolgendo amici e alleati - si pensi alla sicurezza aerea, alla protezione dello strato di ozono o alle armi nucleari - e agendo sempre in modo corretto, senza cercare di sfruttare a nostro esclusivo vantaggio i nostri punti di forza unici. E per quanto riguarda l'IA, dovremo tornare a questo concetto: 'Ehi, l'umanità è tutta sulla stessa barca'". In passato, "solo gli Stati disponevano di squadre per attacchi informatici e potevano concepire minacce come le armi bioterroristiche", ha osservato Gates. "Oggi, piccoli gruppi dotati di IA possono compiere azioni che un tempo erano alla portata solo delle grandi potenze. È dunque la combinazione tra intenzioni malevole e IA a rappresentare una minaccia significativa. Se i governi non imporranno adeguate misure di salvaguardia, assisteremo a gravi conseguenze negative proprio a causa della mancanza di tutele".

items.title: La Corea del Sud ha accusato l’Ucraina di aver reso pubblico un accordo segreto sul trasferimento di due prigionieri nordcoreani
items.content:
La Corea del Sud ha chiesto all’Ucraina spiegazioni e scuse ufficiali per aver reso pubblico il trasferimento di due soldati nordcoreani catturati dall’esercito ucraino. Secondo il governo sudcoreano, i due paesi avevano raggiunto un accordo segreto sul trasferimento, che l’Ucraina ha poi negato. I due soldati erano stati catturati a gennaio del 2025 mentre combattevano al fianco dell’esercito russo nella regione russa di Kursk e avevano chiesto di essere trasferiti in Corea del Sud.

La questione è emersa la scorsa settimana, quando il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky aveva raccontato all’assemblea generale delle Nazioni Unite di aver consegnato i due prigionieri alla Corea del Sud. Poco dopo il presidente sudcoreano Lee Jae-myung aveva pubblicato un post su X dicendo che la divulgazione del trasferimento violava un accordo segreto raggiunto tra i due paesi. Dmytro Lytvyn, consigliere di Zelensky per le comunicazioni, aveva invece negato che esistesse un simile accordo, e aveva detto che sarebbe stato strano trasferire i prigionieri in segreto. Secondo il governo sudcoreano, era stata proprio l’Ucraina a chiedere che il trasferimento rimanesse riservato.

La Corea del Nord è un alleato della Russia, a cui ha fornito truppe e armi per la guerra in Ucraina a seguito di un accordo fra il leader nordcoreano Kim Jong Un e il presidente russo Vladimir Putin. Il numero dei militari nordcoreani inviati a combattere con l’esercito russo non è noto, ma i servizi segreti della Corea del Sud stimano che nel 2025 siano stati 15mila e che ne siano morti circa 6mila.

items.title: Suppletive Reggio Calabria, seggi aperti alle 7, chiudono alle 15
items.summary: Lo spoglio delle schede al via subito dopo. ALle 23 affluenza sotto il 15%
items.content:
Seggi aperti, stamani alle 7, per la seconda giornata di voto per le elezioni suppletive per la Camera nel collegio elettorale Reggio Calabria-Locri. La consultazione interessa complessivamente 71 Comuni. I seggi resteranno aperti sino alle 15 e poi inizierà lo spoglio delle schede.

Alle 23 l'affluenza del collegio 5 Reggio Calabria-Locri per la è stato del 14,97%. Il precedente di 4 anni fa era di 49,4% ma allora era il dato era definitivo, visto che si votava in un solo giorno e quella delle 23 era l'ultima rilevazione di affluenza delle consultazioni. In questa tornata, invece, si vota su due giorni.

items.title: L’estrema destra francese avrà per la prima volta un gruppo al Senato
items.summary: È il risultato più rilevante delle elezioni di domenica in Francia: i partiti di centrodestra e centro hanno comunque mantenuto la maggioranza
items.content:
Alle elezioni del Senato di domenica in Francia la destra ha conservato la maggioranza, mentre i partiti di estrema destra Rassemblement National (RN) e Union des droites pour la République (UDR) hanno ottenuto abbastanza seggi per formare per la prima volta un gruppo parlamentare nella camera alta.

La maggioranza resta in mano al partito di centrodestra dei Républicains (LR) e ai loro alleati centristi, che controllano il Senato dal 2014: il loro peso si è però assai ridotto a vantaggio del RN e dell’UDR. La crescita dell’estrema destra è un segnale notevole anche perché arriva a pochi mesi dalle elezioni presidenziali del 2027, in cui la leader del RN Marine Le Pen è data tra i favoriti.

Prima del voto i Républicains erano già il principale gruppo della camera alta, con 131 senatori, mentre l’Union Centriste ne aveva 72. I Républicains hanno perso tra cinque e sette seggi e dovrebbero quindi averne ora tra 124 e 126. Il numero esatto dipenderà da alcuni eletti che non hanno ancora chiarito a quale gruppo aderiranno.

Domenica erano in palio 178 dei 348 seggi del Senato, in 64 dipartimenti. Il RN aveva già tre senatori e ha ottenuto nove nuovi seggi; insieme ai rappresentanti dell’UDR, che ha eletto due senatori, arriva a 14. Sono quindi più dei dieci necessari per costituire un gruppo parlamentare, il primo dell’estrema destra nella storia del Senato francese.

Il rinnovo del Senato avviene ogni tre anni a suffragio universale indiretto, votano cioè i grandi elettori, per la maggior parte costituiti da amministratori locali: consiglieri comunali, dipartimentali e regionali. Il risultato del RN è legato soprattutto alla sua crescita nelle elezioni comunali di marzo, che gli ha permesso di aumentare il numero di rappresentanti locali. Il Senato ha un ruolo importante nell’approvazione delle leggi, ma non determina la maggioranza che sostiene il governo: è l’Assemblea nazionale, la camera bassa, che può sfiduciarlo.

items.title: Nissan's third generation e-POWER powertrain
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.nissan-global.com/EN/INNOVATION/TECHNOLOGY/ARCHIVE/E_POWER_GEN3/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49872883 Points: 82 # Comments: 103
items.content:
e-POWER is Nissan's unique electric-drive hybrid powertrain that integrates an electric motor with a gasoline engine. Since the system is 100% driven by a high-output motor, drivers can enjoy an EV-like experience with the peace of mind of an onboard gasoline engine for generating energy for the battery.

The third-generation e-POWER system combines a purpose-built engine designed specifically for e-POWER applications. With the ground-up approach of the purpose-built engine, power generation from the engine is further optimized from the previous generation, including activation timing independent of driving conditions and powerband.

The 3rd-gen's new modular approach, called “5-in-1”, integrates five major components to enhance performance, significantly improving fuel efficiency and quietness.

A 5-in-1 modular approach optimizes the packaging of the motor, reducer, inverter, increaser and generator. This approach achieves a high level of efficiency by increasing current flow for greater output and mitigates energy loss.

Improving acceleration and energy efficiency requires higher output, which is achieved by increasing electrical flow. This also brings greater efficiency by reducing energy losses. The 5-in-1 system uses flat wire coils that can be arranged with minimal gaps, allowing higher flow through the motor. The inverter also features a latest generation power module and a double-sided cooling structure that efficiently dissipates heat, improving efficiency particularly at high speeds.

In addition, some models use silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductors in the inverter, which reduce power loss compared with conventional silicon semiconductors. This allows more of the generated electricity to be used to drive the vehicle, reducing the amount of electricity that needs to be generated and helping improve fuel efficiency.

Improving rigidity through integration avoided interference between the resonance points of the vehicle body to further enhance the system's quietness. This also enabled high-precision assembly, reducing runout tolerances of rotating shafts such as motors and gears, thereby suppressing vibration.

By sharing the 3-in-1 EV powertrain and its components, we not only contribute to reducing the number of parts and production investment but also leverage the technologies and expertise of both EV and e-POWER to efficiently drive the development of further optimized electrified powertrains.

There are two types of power-generation-focused engines available. By leveraging a purpose-built onboard engine for power generation, Nissan engineers have achieved a highly efficient powertrain design that significantly improves fuel economy over previous e-POWER applications. A contributor of this is an engine that can maintain a stable combustion cycle.

In general, to improve engine efficiency, it is important to increase the compression ratio and raise the EGR *1 ratio, which recirculates and mixes exhaust gas with the air intake system. Since a typical engine operates across a wide RPM range depending on driving conditions, it is difficult to maintain a stable and optimal combustion cycle.

Nissan's purpose-built engines can operate at a constant speed and maintain stable combustion thanks to their long-stroke design that creates a strong in-cylinder flow (tumble flow). This enables combustion stability even with a high compression ratio and high EGR rate.

To further improve fuel efficiency and output, ZR15DDTe engine uses Nissan's unique STARC *2 concept paired with a large turbocharger.

The STARC concept is the embodiment of research findings that highlight the importance of controlling airflow toward the spark plug inside the combustion chamber to improve ignition. The concept involves managing airflow so that the discharge channel from the spark plug remains stable, guiding combustion effectively and providing a stable combustion even with a high EGR rate.

By using cold spray technology to integrate the valve seat into the engine's intake port, the ideal port shape is achieved, allowing air to be forcefully directed into the cylinder with a strong tumble flow. Additionally, the piston crown is precisely shaped to maintain tumble flow during compression, thus ensuring ignition with a strong spark and stable combustion.

The large turbocharger forces a substantial amount of compressed exhaust gas and air into the cylinder, boosting output while also improving the engine's thermal efficiency.

Advanced control technology supports the powerful and quiet driving that is characteristic of motor drive

Further commonize and modularize core EV and e-POWER components, with the goal of reducing the cost of e-POWER to that of ICE vehicles by 2026

e-POWER's internal combustion engine achieves 50% thermal efficiency

Efficient, fixed-point operation is achieved by restricting the engine's operating range, which is only possible for an engine that is dedicated to electricity generation

The world's first cold spray valve seat structure supporting high efficiency in e-POWER dedicated generator engines

items.title: Owed a billion dollars in Nvidia stock
items.summary: Article URL: https://colo.to/nvidia-stock-narrative.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49872723 Points: 784 # Comments: 326
items.content:
It is not widely known, but I was invited to join the Technical Advisory Board of NVIDIA in 1993 by Jensen (at that time, sans leather jacket) 1 . In September 1993, I was granted 25,000 options, "in a series of quarterly installments so that all shares shall vest upon the expiration of one year from Grant Date." 2

This invitation followed a meeting I had with Jensen, Curtis Priem, and Chris Malachowsky on my houseboat, the SS Vallejo, in Sausalito. I'd done a fair bit of work with Curtis circa 1990, when he was at Sun Microsystems, architect of the SPARCstation GX chip. Sun was one of the companies supporting my early virtual reality company, Sense8 Corporation. The Sun GX was blazingly fast at blitting polygons - some 50k/second - and we'd ported Sense8's VR rendering to it. Subsequently, I implemented bilinear texture mapping using the Intel i750 DVI chip.

But what caught Curtis's attention in 1993, and caused him to bring the other NVIDIA founders to visit me for a demo, was my fast implementation of biquadratic texture mapping. Details are in US5796426A and subsequent patents.

Curtis understood the potential of non-linear texture mapping to differentiate NVIDIA's first product, the NV1, from the competition.

I worked for while, quite casually, with Curtis on porting my biquadratic texture mapping to their hardware, and wrote the code for an Intel-sponsored VR string-quartet demo on prototype NVIDIA hardware - actually a GX card in a PCI adapter - shown at the Guggenheim SoHo in 1993.

When the NV1 finally shipped in 1995, Microsoft decided, for reasons of their own, not to support quadratic texture mapping, or even quads, in their just-released DirectX toolkit - triangles only. This had a devastating effect on NVIDIA's finances and prospects, and the company laid off a large percentage of its staff.

Then, in April 1996 - by which time I'd expatriated to the Kingdom of Tonga and was working on various internet startup schemes - NVIDIA's CFO wrote me a letter stating that 15,625 shares of my stock options had vested, and that I was required to exercise them. 3 I did, and then forgot all about it.

Fast-forward to 2024. I'm sitting with a day-trader friend, surrounded by screens all blaring news about NVIDIA, the Most Important Company on Earth. So I went home and dug through my folder of old documents.

Imagine my surprise: according to the duly signed option agreement, my options were meant to vest over four quarters, not four years, as both NVIDIA's CFO and their outside counsel, Cooley, had asserted back in 1996. The math is clear: 15,625 of 25,000 shares is 62.5% , exactly what you'd expect after ten quarters of a four-year vesting schedule. On the one-year schedule the agreement actually specified, all 25,000 shares should have vested well before that letter was even written.

With the stock's many splits - a cumulative 480x to date - my missing 9,375 shares are now 4,500,000 shares. A handsome enough pile that I engaged formidable attorneys Allan Steyer of Steyer Lowenthal, and Chris Burke of Korein Tillery, to explore the issue. Consummate advocates, letterheads with substantial gravitas.

After about a year of my attorneys and NVIDIA's in-house and outside counsel sending letters back and forth citing case law and blustering, I mentioned to my attorneys that, as I was growing elderly and there seemed to be no end to this exchange of letters, perhaps they could meet and settle. NVIDIA did not dispute the authenticity of the option agreement, only that my claims were long since time-barred.

The meeting was held with great professionalism, but Cooley's answer was, in essence, "so sue us." After much soul-searching, deliberation, and gnashing of teeth, my attorneys and I concluded that the statute of limitations was against us. Because of the thirty-odd years that had passed while I "sat on my rights," it seemed unlikely we'd make it past a motion to dismiss.

I offer this in the spirit of a cautionary tale. I'm sure there are lessons here for those with a more phlegmatic personality than mine. Here in the land of the free, it turns out a company only has to honor its contractual obligations for a little while.

Has anyone else discovered a similar vesting surprise, decades later? And how was it resolved?

I remain sanguine, and amused. As the Emperor Septimius Severus quipped: "Omnia fui, nihil expedit."

items.title: Shipwreck uncovered on Nantucket island during nor'easter storm
items.summary: The so-called nor'easter storm has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, local media says.
items.content:
A powerful nor'easter storm has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, local media said.

The wreckage discovered on a beach on Sunday is believed to be part of the "Warren Sawyer" – which ran aground near Nantucket in 1884, according to the Nantucket Current.

Fragments of the wooden ship were also discovered in 2022 and 2023.

Heavy rainfall and dangerous coastal flooding have hit parts of north-eastern US, with more than 160,000 households experiencing power cuts.

items.title: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey
items.summary: Tens of millions of people from Maine to Virginia found themselves in the path of the powerful weather system.
items.content:
Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.

The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.

States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine.

In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree.

The man has been identified as 56-year-old Leighton Brown, an employee of the New York City Housing Authority.

According to local news, he was walking through east Brooklyn neighbourhood working an extra shift when the deadly incident occurred.

"We mourn deeply for the loss of Leighton Brown, a NYCHA employee who faithfully served Brooklyn residents and who was known for his warm personality," the Office of the NYC Public Advocate wrote on social media.

The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage.

More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware.

A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.

NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."

In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines.

"Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."

In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida.

A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.

The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead.

Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather.

Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.

items.title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day organiser
items.summary: World News Day aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.
items.content:
More than 1,000 news providers around the world have signed up to support World News Day on Monday, which aims to promote the role of journalism at a time when organisers say the industry faces an "existential threat".

Participating media organisations, including the New York Times, Reuters and the Kyiv Independent, are sharing editorials, ads and cartoons to highlight the value of "trusted journalism".

Trust in news dropped to a new low globally in 2026, according to the Reuters Institute's latest Digital News Report , which noted that people are increasingly turning to social media and AI chatbots for news.

Branko Brkic, co-organiser of World News Day, said media organisations that were once rivals must work together, adding: "If we do not change the game, we are just not going to exist."

World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.

It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer".

Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said.

In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom , external also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news.

But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said.

Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond.

"The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said.

"If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill."

Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society.

"We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said.

"We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts."

The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media".

Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us."

items.title: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
items.summary: In a system often marked by red tape and exhausting delays, officers seen to be following the rules get adulation.
items.content:
Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years.

The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food.

He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged.

These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state.

Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments.

But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs?

In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post.

So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic.

"What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal.

For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds.

Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that.

One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules.

Kiran Bedi , the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported , external his decision).

Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020.

These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare.

Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention.

"Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible."

For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process.

Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints.

"What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says.

But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities.

Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases.

Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules.

Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay.

This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh.

Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties.

Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands.

"They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says.

She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper.

In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election.

He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after".

But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye.

The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward.

Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says.

Social media has also changed how quickly an officer can become a public sensation.

An action once limited to a district can now be filmed, shared and viewed by millions within hours.

"Social media can turn an official into a national talking point almost overnight," Sundar says.

That is partly what happened with Mundhe, whose inspection videos have turned routine enforcement into a widely watched spectacle.

Speaking to the BBC last month, he said his actions were driven by public-health concerns and that businesses complying with rules had nothing to fear.

For Mundhe, the attention is beside the point. The rules already exist and his job is simply to enforce them.

But the public fascination is about more than just one officer.

When basic government functions are carried out visibly and consistently, they can seem extraordinary - particularly because so many people have come to expect otherwise.

items.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
items.summary: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.
items.content:
"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."

The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.

Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.

It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.

We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.

Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting.

It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire.

"Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.

He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals.

"I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."

He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.

At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach.

Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.

The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.

Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.

Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.

We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.

About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.

As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.

We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.

Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.

Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.

Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.

There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line.

"It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.

The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.

Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.

In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.

Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.

She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.

A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.

About 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.

We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.

Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day.

"We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.

Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain.

"We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.

Fatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."

Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.

She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said.

"I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."

A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.

On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.

It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.

items.title: Lunar Terminator Paradox
items.summary: Article URL: https://notes.secretsauce.net/notes/2026/09/27_lunar-terminator-paradox.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49870837 Points: 90 # Comments: 56
items.content:
There's an optical illusion known by names like the "lunar terminator paradox". This has much discussion and descriptions online, but none made sense in my head, so I wrote this program to figure out what was going on. The paradox:

I was camping in the mountains with a friend recently. We were looking up at the sky, just after the sun has set. The moon was clearly pointing up.

After playing with this program , I have clarity: we're looking up at the moon from below. The most pathological case is a full moon. Let's say the moon is on the horizon: elevation=0. If we're looking at this low moon, and the moon is full, the sun is directly behind us. The moon is fully illuminated, and we see 100% of the moon disc lit up.

Now, what happens if the moon is not at the horizon, but higher up at the sky? Effectively, the sun is infinitely far away, so the same part of the moon is lit up. But we're now looking at the moon from below, and we would see some of the dark side on the bottom edge. I.e. the moon appears bright at the top, but has a dark slice missing at the bottom: it points up! Even at sunset.

This is the most clearly weird case. A half-moon has no paradoxical behavior, and the more full the moon, the more clearly we can observe the bright moon pointing up despite the sun being down.

I produce two plots. At 3/4-full moon at sunset we look at the moon as it rises from the horizon all the way up to the zenith:

If the moon is at the horizon (elevation = 0), we see the expected 3/4-lit disc. As the moon rises, we see more and more of its bottom, and thus more and more dark areas show up: It clearly points up at sunset!

We can also move the sun around. Let's say the moon is 60deg up; let's move the sun from new-moon to a full-moon:

In the darkest configuration, we can still see a lit crescent on the bottom: the illumination is all on the opposite side, but we can see a slice of the illuminated back side. As the sun swings around, we see more and more of the moon. At azimuth = 90deg, we have a half-lit moon. Past that, more and more of the moon is visible, always pointing up.

This was also a super interesting study of the current state of AI tools. As I was writing this and debugging, I would talk to Claude and Gemini about how this worked and what I should be seeing. They were both completely unable to comprehend this, and would make infinite circular arguments. Clearly they read some incomplete explanations on the internet (as I have), and lack the reasoning capability necessary to distill it into something resembling "understanding". AGI is not here yet.

items.title: When did Google get so weird?
items.summary: Article URL: https://sancho.bearblog.dev/google-weird/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49870367 Points: 1397 # Comments: 753
items.content:
I recently had an experience while doing a simple Google search that was so profoundly weird that it stopped me in my tracks.

Understanding this Google search experience involves understanding a niche mid-2010s basketball meme, so bear with me for a minute. In 2014 the Philadelphia 76ers drafted Dario Saric, who was playing basketball professionally in Turkey at the time. He announced his intention to finish out his contract in Turkey, meaning he wouldn't come to the USA join the Sixers for a couple of years. There was a joke within the fan community that Dario was "never coming over" which became sort of a shibboleth for part of the fanbase.

I saw Dario's name mentioned in an NBA article recently and I wanted to find some of those old funny tweets about him from the 2010s, so I Googled simply "hes never coming over dario". I assumed I would be either find nothing (maybe I was remembering the phrasing wrong) or find old Tweets/Reddit posts from that time.

Instead, Google did what Google does in 2026 and gave me an AI overview. These used to bother me but at this point I'm mostly ok with them, they're sometimes helpful. Here's what the AI Overview said:

Google, a search engine which does not have human emotions , assumed that I had been spurned by a man in my life named Dario and decided what I wanted was an empathetic digital friend. What I wanted was some links, but that's not what Google does in 2026. Expanding the AI overview to see the full answer gave me this:

What in the fucking hell? I think this was the moment I, the frog, noticed the pot had been boiling for a while. In what universe is it Google's job to console me and be an empathetic listener rather than just find what I am looking for on the internet? In what way does this "organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful"? Maybe if I had loaded up a Gemini app with a chat interface this would be somewhat acceptable, but I'm using a search engine! Google has seriously lost the plot.

If I scroll down a few hundred pixels below the AI slop, Google did have exactly what I was looking for:

Regardless of what you think of AI or chatbots, I think it's pretty obvious this is just plain weird. Have we gotten to the point where we have to constantly be in a parasocial dialogue with our computers? Is it so hard to imagine that some parts of search were just fine before LLMs?

I'm not sure how to feel about all of this. Maybe I should go talk to my friend Google, it's always so nice to me.

items.title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
items.summary: Aleksandar Vučić's administration has been dogged by prolonged protests over allegations of corruption.
items.content:
Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption.

Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade.

He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution.

The populist leader's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting.

It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof , killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024.

Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed.

Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress.

A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality .

Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation.

This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year.

Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands.

He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics.

Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected.

Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS.

The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia.

Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade , becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017.

He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment.

items.title: Self-Hosting on the Dark Web
items.summary: Article URL: https://david.alvarezrosa.com/posts/self-hosting-on-the-dark-web/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49870295 Points: 226 # Comments: 84
items.content:
This site is now reachable over Tor as a hidden service, at a .onion address that resolves only inside the Tor network. 1 1 Open it in the Tor Browser . There is no certificate authority, no DNS, and no exposed IP-the address is derived directly from a public key, and the connection is end-to-end encrypted by Tor itself. Tor relays and encrypts your traffic as it passes through thousands of volunteer-run servers, so that no single party can link who you are to what you are doing; a hidden service extends that anonymity to the server itself.

It's built by the nonprofit Tor Project , which advances human rights and freedoms through free software and open networks, so that anyone can use the internet free from tracking, surveillance, and censorship. The network only works because people use it, so consider supporting them or running a relay-your contribution helps millions stay safe and private online every day.

Install Tor and point a hidden service at a local port. Edit /etc/tor/torrc

The directory must be a dedicated, Tor-owned path-not your web root. 2 2 Tor stores the service's private key and hostname file here and insists on owning it ( chmod 700 , user debian-tor ). Point it at your site files and Tor refuses to start. Restart Tor and read the address it generates

Tor forwards the onion's port 80 to 127.0.0.1:8080 , so the web server just needs to listen there. Add an nginx server block for it-no TLS, no HTTP/2, no QUIC, since Tor speaks plain TCP and provides its own encryption.

A static site bakes its base URL into absolute links, so a clearnet build would point visitors back to the clearnet domain even when served over Tor. The fix is to build a second copy with the onion as its base URL

The deploy pipeline does this automatically: every push builds the site once per target-clearnet and Tor-and rsyncs each to its own web root, so the two stay in sync without any manual work. 3 3 See First Steps on a New Server for the underlying machine; the full configuration lives in my homelab repository, and the site's own repository holds the GitHub Actions workflow that builds and deploys the Tor copy.

That's it. Read this site over Tor at dhevt6e4rtgbtr3jh53xrpwmgtilkah6nyjujocsspssrsexc7omxhid.onion .

items.title: Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes
items.summary: Pope Leo spoke to bishops before leading a service attended by thousands of worshippers in France.
items.content:
Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance".

The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.

A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.

The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse.

The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.

"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."

The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.

Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy.

The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement.

"It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added.

The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.

Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.

On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.

During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".

The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech , describing them as "today's Church".

"How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.

The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.

But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.

Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s.

The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK.

Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world.

A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys.

Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church , and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse , but problems remain.

Later on Sunday, the Pope met staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, and took part in a torchlight procession.

It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025.

Popes have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots.

items.title: I mosaici di Rupnik a Lourdes, il velo per il rispetto alle vittime
items.summary: L'artista, ex gesuita, è accusato di abusi. Erano stati inaugurati nel 2008
items.content:
Da quasi vent'anni erano il simbolo del santuario di Lourdes: opere colorate, luminose, con lo sguardo dei personaggi del Vangelo che in qualche modo 'parlava'. Erano i mosaici di Marko Rupnik, l'ex gesuita accusato di abusi da diverse religiose. Per questo era stato anche scomunicato, poi Francesco aveva tolto questa pesante sanzione. Ma alcune vittime vogliono giustizia e ora Rupnik è sotto processo alla Dottrina della Fede.

Che cosa fare delle opere artistiche di una persona accusata di uno dei crimini più odiosi? Il vescovo di Lourdes, Jean-Marc Micas, da tempo ragionava sul fatto che nel santuario mariano si recano a pregare anche vittime di queste violenze. Ed avere come primo impatto la grandiosa opera di una persona accusata era un'offesa. La decisione è andata per gradi: prima è stato deciso di non illuminarli la sera. Ora, per la visita del Papa, sono stati coperti. Una decisione che appare irreversibile. Verosimilmente si arriverà alla rimozione.

Inaugurati nel 2008, per il centocinquantesimo anniversario delle apparizioni mariane, rappresentavano i Misteri della Luce, le cinque scene del rosario introdotte da Giovanni Paolo II. Erano in tutte le fotografie di gruppo dei pellegrini, erano la prima cosa che saltava all'occhio entrando dall'ingresso principale e, la sera, quando il popolo di Lourdes si riunisce in processione, cantando e pregando, erano il punto finale della celebrazione, occupando quasi l'intera facciata della basilica del rosario.

Già a luglio del 2024 il vescovo Micas aveva detto: "Sarebbe preferibile rimuovere questi mosaici". Poi la decisione di andare per tappe: prima la non illuminazione, ora sono stati coperti con dei teli del colore della basilica, tornando dunque all'impatto precedente al 2008. Ma già si immagina la loro rimozione. Il portavoce della Conferenza episcopale francese, mons. Pierre-Antonie Bozo oggi ha detto: "È stato un primo passo, dopo bisognerà proporre qualcosa di bello, abbiamo degli artisti per questo".

Le vittime di Rupnik hanno recentemente espresso la loro soddisfazione per questa decisione del santuario mariano sui Pirenei francesi. Ma Rupnik è un po' il Caravaggio dei nostri tempi e il paragone riguarda non solo la diffusione delle sue opere ma anche il fatto che l'artista del 1600 fu accusato di risse, possesso illegale di armi e finanche di omicidio. E se a Lourdes sono stati coperti, i mosaici di Rupnik, un paio di settimane fa sono stati invece inaugurati al santuario di Nostra Signora di Aparecida, in Brasile.

Sono dappertutto queste opere, si calcola in duecento luoghi di culto nel mondo, da Fatima (Portogallo) a Cracovia in Polonia, da Washington a Manresa in Spagna. E finanche dentro il Vaticano e il Laterano dove intere cappelle sono coperte dalle tessere che arrivavano dal Centro Aletti, la fucina delle opere d'arte dell'ex gesuita. E costellavano le pagine del Vangelo dei siti vaticani fino a quando Leone XIV ha chiesto di cancellarle tutte. Dopo Lourdes, con il Papa fotografato davanti alla basilica 'spoglia' di quelle opere, gli altri seguiranno la stessa strada?

items.title: Aleksandar Vučić si è dimesso da presidente della Serbia, per provare a diventare primo ministro
items.content:
Come aveva preannunciato a fine giugno, il presidente della Serbia Aleksandar Vučić si è dimesso dal proprio ruolo, in vista delle elezioni anticipate in programma per il prossimo 25 ottobre. Le elezioni serviranno per rinnovare il parlamento serbo: Vučić, che è conservatore e nazionalista, si ricandiderà con il suo partito (il Partito Progressista Serbo, di centrodestra), con l’obiettivo di diventare primo ministro. Il suo secondo mandato da presidente sarebbe scaduto il prossimo maggio, e la Costituzione gli avrebbe comunque impedito di candidarsi per un terzo.

Vučić governa dal 2014 in modo sempre più autoritario, e lui e il suo partito sono stati accusati di corruzione, legami con la criminalità organizzata e di aver progressivamente eroso le libertà nel paese. La sua popolarità è calata in particolare dopo il crollo di una tettoia della stazione ferroviaria di Novi Sad , la seconda città serba, che nel novembre del 2024 provocò la morte di 16 persone. Il disastro è diventato un simbolo della corruzione diffusa nella classe politica serba, e in questi due anni ha provocato numerose proteste antigovernative .

Formalmente in Serbia il primo ministro ha più poteri del presidente, ma durante i suoi mandati Vučić è comunque riuscito a dettare almeno in parte la propria agenda. Il ruolo di presidente verrà temporaneamente ricoperto da Ana Brnabić, che è la presidente del parlamento uscente, appartiene al partito di Vučić ed è una sua collaboratrice storica: dopo le elezioni del 25 ottobre, verranno indette anche le elezioni presidenziali.

items.title: Imp is a full port of DSPy to the BEAM
items.summary: https://hex.pm/packages/imp https://dspy.ai/current/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49869995 Points: 81 # Comments: 7
items.content:
Declarative, self-improving language-model programs for Elixir.

Imp is a full port of DSPy to the BEAM. You describe what each language-model step takes and returns, choose how it thinks, and let an optimizer improve it against examples of what good looks like. You get signatures, modules, optimizers, agent loops and retrieval, running with the reliability and concurrency of OTP.

DSPy makes each call to a model a declared, typed function that you can measure and improve. On the BEAM, an agent is a process: it keeps its own state, receives messages, and runs under a supervisor alongside the rest of your application. With both, you can build anything from one typed call to many long-running agents, and improve each part by measuring it.

You never write a prompt or a parser. Imp builds the prompt from the signature, checks the reply against it, and gives you typed fields: kind is always one of the three values, or the call returns an error. To make the same task reason first, use Imp.chain_of_thought/2 ; to give it tools, use Imp.react/3 . The signature stays the same.

Give Imp labeled examples and a metric, and it scores the program and optimizes it. You need three lists of issues you have already labeled: trainset , which the optimizer learns from; valset , which it uses to choose between the programs it tries; and testset , which you score on before and after. strong_lm is a more capable model that GEPA uses to read failures and write new instructions.

GEPA runs the program, reads where it failed, and rewrites its instructions. Other optimizers choose worked examples (LabeledFewShot, BootstrapFewShot), search over combinations of instructions and examples (MIPROv2), learn rules and examples from the program's own better and worse attempts (SIMBA), or train the model's weights (fine-tuning, GRPO). The result is a new program whose instructions and examples you can read, save as JSON, and review as a diff.

A tool is an Elixir function. Imp.react/3 builds an agent that calls tools until it can answer. This one reads web pages with Req. Imp depends on Req; if your own code calls it, as this tool does, add {:req, "~> 0.6"} to your dependencies:

Imp.call/2 runs a program in your process. Imp.start_run/3 runs it as its own supervised process instead, so you can watch it, stop it, and decide which tool calls it may make:

The optimizers work on agents too. GEPA reflects on whole agent runs and rewrites the instructions that steer them. Optimize Anything rewrites any text or JSON you can score, such as an agent's tool descriptions.

Imp needs Elixir 1.19 or later and a C and C++ compiler, for the native code in two dependencies (jaxon and erlexec). The first compile needs network access, because erlexec's build fetches rebar3 plugins. It reaches models through ReqLLM , so any provider ReqLLM supports works.

Imp 0.5 is experimental and is its first release on Hex. Its API may still change, and its optimizers need large-scale benchmarking. Bug reports and pull requests are welcome.
